lesson.title: Who Wins the Fight? Ranking Metal Reactivity with the Activity Series
lesson.summary: The activity series ranks metals from most to least reactive, giving you a fast way to predict whether a single replacement reaction will actually happen before you ever try to balance it.
lesson.body:
Single Replacement taught you the pattern A + BC -> AC + B, where a free element takes the place of another element already combined in a compound. But writing that pattern on paper does not guarantee the reaction actually occurs. If you drop a piece of copper into a solution of zinc sulfate, nothing happens, even though Cu + ZnSO4 -> CuSO4 + Zn looks perfectly reasonable as a chemical equation. The missing piece is reactivity: some metals give up their electrons more readily than others, and a less reactive metal simply cannot pull electrons away from the ions of a more reactive metal.

The activity series solves this by ranking metals, from experiments, according to how readily they lose electrons to form cations. A simplified classroom version, from most to least reactive, reads: potassium, calcium, sodium, magnesium, aluminum, zinc, iron, lead, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold. Hydrogen is included as a reference point, since it tells you which metals can displace H2 gas from acids. More complete versions of the series add additional metals, including lithium, near the very top. The governing rule is simple: a metal can displace any metal, or hydrogen, that sits below it in the series from a dissolved compound, but it cannot displace anything above it.

It is tempting to assume this ranking is just ionization energy in disguise, and ionization energy is indeed part of the story: a metal that loses its outermost electron easily, meaning it has a low first ionization energy, tends to be a more willing electron donor and a more reactive metal. But the activity series is measured experimentally in aqueous solution, not calculated from gas phase ionization energies alone, and the two orders do not match perfectly. Lithium, for example, has a higher first ionization energy than sodium or potassium, yet it sits at or near the top of most activity series because its very small, highly charged ion releases an enormous amount of energy when it becomes surrounded by water molecules, its hydration energy, which more than compensates for the harder ionization step. The lesson is that periodic trends give you useful intuition, but the activity series itself is an empirical ranking built from real displacement experiments.

Apply the rule to zinc metal placed in a copper(II) sulfate solution: Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s). Zinc sits above copper in the activity series, so zinc is more reactive and displaces copper from solution. The equation is already balanced: 1 zinc, 1 copper, and 1 sulfate group on each side. In the lab, you would see the blue color of the CuSO4 solution fade as reddish copper metal plates out. Reverse the setup, copper metal placed in zinc sulfate solution, and nothing happens, because copper sits below zinc and cannot displace it. This single comparison, checking positions in the activity series, is often all you need to predict whether a single replacement reaction will proceed.
